content_voiceover: Here the Hokusai VTE Cancer trial results are split into its two separate endpoints, recurrent venous thromboembolism on the left and major bleeding on the right, which is the more clinically useful way to interpret this trial. For recurrent VTE, edoxaban trended lower than dalteparin, but the difference did not reach statistical significance, with a p value of zero point zero nine. For major bleeding, however, edoxaban had a significantly higher rate than dalteparin, with a p value of zero point zero four, and you can see that separation clearly in the right hand curve where the blue edoxaban line climbs well above the red dalteparin line after about day ninety. So the net take home is that edoxaban was noninferior overall for the composite endpoint, largely because it trended toward fewer recurrent clots, but that benefit came at the cost of more bleeding, particularly in patients with gastrointestinal cancers, which is a detail worth remembering for boards since it shaped later guideline caution about DOAC use in luminal GI malignancies.
keypoints: Recurrent VTE: edoxaban trended lower than dalteparin, not significant (p=0.09)
Major bleeding: edoxaban significantly higher than dalteparin (p=0.04)
Bleeding excess mostly driven by GI cancer patients
Net effect: noninferior composite, but bleeding tradeoff with edoxaban
Informed later caution against DOACs in luminal GI malignancy
keypoint_voiceover: The two curves separate the composite into components. Edoxaban trended toward less recurrent VTE without reaching significance, but had significantly more major bleeding, largely driven by GI cancers, which is why guidelines later cautioned against DOACs in luminal GI malignancy.
